newsitem.title: FRANCE: Euro-rights panel rejects Tapie, Touvier appeals.
newsitem.headline: Euro-rights panel rejects Tapie, Touvier appeals.

text.p: The European Commission of Human Rights rejected on Thursday pleas by bankrupt politician Bernard Tapie and the late war criminal Paul Touvier that they had been unfairly convicted in France.

Tapie, a former cabinet minister and soccer boss who built up a substantial business, sport and political empire only to lose it, has accused the French justice system of targeting him for political reasons in a series of corruption cases.
He has been convicted of tax fraud and rigging a league game involving the Marseille soccer team which he formerly owned.
French courts have also declared him bankrupt and stripped him of his seat in the French National Assembly and he now faces losing his last political job -- his seat in the European Parliament.
Touvier, the only Frenchman to be jailed for World War Two crimes against humanity, died last July in a prison hospital after a long battle with cancer, aged 81.
He had been serving an eight-month sentence for ordering the execution of Jewish hostages in Rilleux-la-Pape, central France, while serving as intelligence chief of the region's pro-Nazi militia.
The commission screens cases for the European Court of Human Rights, also based in Strasbourg, eastern France. Both the commission and the court are a part of the 40-nation Council of Europe.
